inDevelopment.meta: Not yet recruiting · n=60 · single site · start Jul 2026 · primary completion Aug 2028
inDevelopment.title: Intradiscal rhGDF-6 for lumbar disc degeneration: safety, tolerability and preliminary efficacy
inDevelopment.frame: Cartago Biotech. Open-label, single administration, high- and low-dose arms. A growth-factor injection aimed at the disc itself rather than at decompression or fusion.
inDevelopment.forWork: If intradiscal biologics reach the clinic, the comparator will be the outcomes you already measure. Your PROM and MCID infrastructure across ACDF and lumbar decompression is exactly the benchmark a trial like this needs, and nobody can build that retrospectively.
inDevelopment.short: Intradiscal growth factor for disc degeneration, n=60 first-in-human. Your PROM thresholds would be the benchmark.

inDevelopment.meta: Recruiting · n=25 · 2 sites · started Apr 2026 · primary completion Oct 2027
inDevelopment.title: LDGraft in single-level lumbar interbody fusion
inDevelopment.frame: Locate Bio. A bone graft substitute in single-level lumbar interbody fusion, small and early.
inDevelopment.forWork: Graft material is the variable your cost analysis did not isolate. A single-level fusion cohort with graft cost and outcome together would extend that paper's method from approach to implant.
inDevelopment.short: LDGraft in single-level lumbar fusion, n=25. Graft cost is the variable your cost paper didn't isolate.

inDevelopment.meta: Not yet recruiting · n=90 · start Jun 2026 · primary completion May 2027
inDevelopment.title: Effect of obesity phenotype on intra-abdominal pressure, intraoperative bleeding and perioperative complications in major lumbar spinal surgery
inDevelopment.frame: Marmara University. Measures intra-abdominal pressure via bladder catheter and relates obesity phenotype to bleeding and complications.
inDevelopment.forWork: This is the mechanism your obesity work observes from the outcome side. Your two-level CDR study found comparable PROM trajectories in obese patients; this asks what is happening intraoperatively. A phenotype variable — not just BMI — may be what distinguishes the patients who do differ.
inDevelopment.short: Obesity phenotype vs intraoperative pressure and bleeding. The mechanism behind your BMI outcome work.

inDevelopment.meta: Recruiting · n=165 · 3 sites · started Oct 2025 · primary completion Oct 2026
inDevelopment.title: Spontaneous correction of sagittal imbalance after isolated decompression without corrective fusion for lumbar spinal stenosis
inDevelopment.frame: N.N. Priorov Centre, Moscow. Tests whether sagittal imbalance corrects itself after decompression alone, without adding fusion.
inDevelopment.forWork: Directly relevant to decompression-only decision-making. Your workers' compensation decompression cohort already tracks ODI and VAS over two years; adding sagittal parameters to it would answer the same question in a US population with far better PROM capture.
inDevelopment.short: Does sagittal imbalance self-correct after decompression alone? n=165. Your decompression cohort could answer it too.

inDevelopment.meta: Not yet recruiting · n=300 · start Jan 2026 · primary completion Jun 2026
inDevelopment.title: Safety of cervical spine fusion with NMP graft material
inDevelopment.frame: Red Rock Regeneration. Natural Matrix Protein fibres in cervical interbody fusion, safety only.
inDevelopment.forWork: A chart review of 300 with safety endpoints and no PROMs. Your ACDF database carries the patient-reported side this is missing, which makes it the obvious partner for anyone wanting to know whether a graft changes how patients actually feel.
inDevelopment.short: NMP graft in cervical fusion, n=300, safety only. Your ACDF PROMs are what it lacks.

newPapers.meta: Eur Spine J · Oct 2026 · Verna, Hughes et al. (Hospital for Special Surgery)
newPapers.title: Preoperative disability is independently associated with postoperative care intensity following anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
newPapers.frame: 333 patients, 299 analysed. A composite care-intensity score from length of stay, delayed extubation and stepdown admission. Preoperative NDI was independently associated with greater care intensity (IRR 1.11 per 10 points, P=.018), as were number of levels fused (IRR 1.54 per level) and age. Patient expectations and PHQ-8 were not.
newPapers.versus: Extends rather than contradicts. Your ACDF MCID-failure paper found preoperative VAS-neck and foraminal stenosis predicted early MCID failure, with better preoperative physical function and mental health protective. They find baseline disability predicts in-hospital resource use as well as patient-reported recovery — the same preoperative variable reaching a different outcome.
newPapers.forWork: Your lumbar decompression work already shows severe baseline ODI predicts greater improvement, not worse. Pairing that with their finding would address the live question for outpatient ACDF pathways: does high preoperative disability argue against same-day surgery, or for it? You have the PROM depth to answer that and they do not report MCID.
newPapers.short: Baseline NDI predicts in-hospital care intensity after ACDF, not just PROMs — extends your MCID-failure work.

newPapers.meta: J Neurosurg Spine · Oct 2026 · Tu, Wu et al. (Taipei Veterans General)
newPapers.title: Hypermobile cervical disc arthroplasty: clinical and radiological outcomes at minimum 2-year follow-up
newPapers.frame: 114 single-level C5-6 ProDisc-C patients, minimum 24 months. 28.9% were hypermobile (ROM ≥15°, mean 17.8°). Both groups improved significantly on VAS neck, VAS arm, NDI and mJOA with no difference at final follow-up. Heterotopic ossification 12.1% vs 19.6% (P=.331), adjacent segment degeneration 3.0% vs 12.3% (P=.127). No device failure.
newPapers.versus: Consistent in shape with your CDR findings — a patient characteristic that looks as though it ought to matter, and does not. Your two-level CDR study found obesity did not change PROM trajectory or MCID achievement; your ASA paper found higher ASA class did not predict worse outcomes. Three different variables, same answer.
newPapers.forWork: They have segmental ROM and no MCID; you have MCID and, in a two-level series, a question they did not ask. A two-level CDR cohort stratified by postoperative ROM would be genuinely new — their data is single-level C5-6 only, and their adjacent-segment signal (3.0% vs 12.3%) is underpowered rather than absent.
newPapers.short: Hypermobility after CDA didn't change outcomes — the same 'variable that shouldn't matter' pattern as your obesity and ASA papers.

newPapers.meta: Int J Spine Surg · Oct 2026 · Patwardhan, Zigler et al. (Hines VA / Loyola / Texas Back)
newPapers.title: Likelihood of achieving physiological mobility after cervical disc arthroplasty: motion restoration versus motion preservation
newPapers.frame: Secondary analysis of 131 levels from the M6-C trial. Splits the question in two: restoring physiological ROM (5-16°) to segments that were hypo- or hypermobile beforehand (71%, 30/42), versus preserving it where it already was (82%, 73/89). Combined likelihood 79%.
newPapers.versus: Different measure, same clinical decision. Your CDR papers predict who does well from patient factors — BMI, ASA class. This predicts what the implant will do mechanically from the preoperative ROM. The two together are what a patient is actually asking.
newPapers.forWork: Worth noting this group is local — Hines VA and Loyola, Maywood. Their framing of restoration versus preservation is a clean way to report motion, and your single-surgeon two-level series could apply it to a level count they have no data on.
newPapers.short: Splits CDA motion into restoration vs preservation; 79% achieve physiological ROM. Local group, Hines VA.

newPapers.meta: Orthop Surg · Sep 2026 · Zhao, Wang et al. (West China Hospital)
newPapers.title: Effect of keeping the Caspar retractor during Prestige LP cervical disc implantation on intra- and postoperative outcomes
newPapers.frame: 55 patients. Keeping the retractor in during endplate preparation and implantation reduced Cobb-angle fluctuation (P=.001), fluoroscopy exposures (P=.044) and implantation time (P=.017), and allowed larger prostheses (P<.001) — against the manufacturer's own instruction to relax or remove it. More functional spinal unit height loss at 6 months (P=.002); subsidence and heterotopic ossification unchanged.
newPapers.versus: A different kind of finding from yours: a technical modification with resource consequences rather than a patient-factor analysis. But fluoroscopy count and operative time are inputs to exactly the cost model you built for endoscopic versus tubular versus open discectomy.
newPapers.forWork: Your cost paper priced approaches. This prices a step within an approach. Extending that method to CDR technique variables — retractor handling, fluoroscopy count, implantation time — would be a natural second paper, and you already have the costing framework and the single-surgeon volume to do it.
newPapers.short: Keeping the Caspar retractor cut fluoroscopy and implantation time, against the manufacturer's instruction.

alsoNoted.text: Your own group's meta-analysis of metagenomic next-generation sequencing versus culture in native pyogenic spinal infections (1,227 patients, 12 studies) reported pooled sensitivity 89.7% and diagnostic yield 69-90% against 27-45% for culture. Listed here because it is the most citable thing in your recent output for anyone searching culture-negative spinal infection, and it has no comparator paper yet in this window.

Power-drill fluoroscopy-controlled freehand pedicle screws matched navigation for accuracy (97.8% vs 93.5%, P=.02) with a third of the radiation, in a propensity-matched cohort from St. Gallen that you co-authored. Radiation dose as an outcome sits alongside your cost work as the other under-reported cost of technique choice.
